title: How a Wolf Became Your Dog. #1 Was Hiding in a Fox's Brain
description: Your dog is the same species as a wolf, so where did the wolf go? Puppy-dog-eye muscles, starch genes, a stare that bonds you both, a 15,800-year-old puppy confirmed by DNA, and a brand-new Cornell study (Nov 2, 2026) that looked inside the brains of tame foxes. Five secrets, counted down to #1. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Your dog's ancestors were wolves. And scientists just found where the wolf went.

scenes.label: Same species
scenes.say: Okay, think about the dog on your couch right now. Same species as a gray wolf. Same basic body plan.

scenes.label: Wolf vs dog
scenes.say: But a wolf avoids your eyes. A wolf won't beg for toast. So what changed, and how fast did it happen?

scenes.label: Saved for #1
scenes.say: And here's the wild part. The newest clue came out this week, and it was hiding inside a fox's brain. That's number one.

scenes.label: Bones, muscles, hormones
scenes.say: Here's a hint. Scientists can now read the answer in ancient bones, in tiny face muscles, and even in hormones.
So today we're counting down five secrets of how a wolf became your dog, from cute to honestly kind of spooky.

scenes.label: Chose us or built?
scenes.say: Quick question before we start. Do you think dogs chose us, or did we build them? Lock in your answer.

scenes.label: Puppy dog eyes
scenes.say: Number five. Puppy dog eyes. You know that look. The sad little eyebrow lift right before your sandwich disappears.

scenes.label: Dog vs wolf heads
scenes.say: Scientists at the University of Portsmouth dissected dog and wolf heads to see what makes that look possible.

scenes.label: Inner eyebrow muscle
scenes.say: They found a tiny muscle that raises the inner eyebrow. In dogs, it was there every single time.

scenes.label: Missing in wolves
scenes.say: In wolves? It wasn't. Wolves basically don't have the muscle for that face.
Then they filmed dogs and wolves. Dogs made the eyebrow move more often and harder. The strongest versions came only from dogs.

scenes.label: Looks like sadness
scenes.say: Here's the thing. That move makes a dog look younger, and a bit like a sad human face. It hits us right in the heart.

scenes.label: We picked the faces
scenes.say: So the researchers think people simply favored the dogs with the most expressive eyebrows. We picked those faces without noticing.
In other words, your dog's begging face might be thousands of years of us falling for the same trick.

scenes.label: Built for our food
scenes.say: Number four. Your dog can eat your food. And a wolf really isn't built for that.

scenes.label: 10 diet genes
scenes.say: When scientists compared dog and wolf DNA, they found ten genes linked to digesting starch and fat that had changed in dogs.

scenes.label: Starch enzyme
scenes.say: The big one is a gene for amylase. That's the enzyme that breaks down starch, like bread, rice and porridge.

scenes.label: ~11 copies
scenes.say: Most dogs carry lots of copies of that gene. Around eleven in the typical dog in one worldwide study.

scenes.label: Only ~3 copies
scenes.say: But some dogs from the Arctic and Australia carry only about three. Their people mostly didn't farm.

scenes.label: Farming changed dogs
scenes.say: And that's the clue. Where humans started growing grain, their dogs got better at eating it. Our leftovers literally rewrote their genes.
But wait. Dogs were living with us long before anyone farmed anything. So how far back does this really go?

scenes.label: The stare
scenes.say: Number three. When your dog stares at you, something happens inside both of your bodies. Both of them.

scenes.label: Stare = threat
scenes.say: Remember, for wolves, a long stare is usually a threat. Wolves tend to avoid eye contact with people.

scenes.label: Bonding hormone
scenes.say: So Japanese scientists measured oxytocin, a hormone linked to bonding, in dog owners before and after playtime.

scenes.label: Both go up
scenes.say: Dogs that gazed at their owners longer raised the owners' oxytocin. And the dogs' own levels went up too.

scenes.label: A loop
scenes.say: Then it gets weirder. When dogs got a sniff of oxytocin, they gazed at their owners more. And the owners' levels rose again.

scenes.label: Not in wolves
scenes.say: They tried it with wolves raised by hand. Even after half an hour together, no mutual gaze and no rise in oxytocin.
Scientists call it a loop. Your dog looks at you, you both feel closer, so you look back. Wolves just don't do it.
So that feeling when your dog stares at you? That might be one of the oldest friendships on Earth working exactly as designed.

scenes.label: Halfway
scenes.say: Okay, we're halfway. Next up is the oldest dog ever confirmed by DNA. And where it was found is kind of eerie.

scenes.label: How old?
scenes.say: Number two. How old is that friendship? This year, ancient DNA gave a brand new answer.

scenes.label: 3 puppies, 2004
scenes.say: In 2004, archaeologists in central Turkey found three puppies in a pit, placed right above a human grave.

scenes.label: Wolf or dog?
scenes.say: But the bones were too small to tell. Wolf pups or dog pups? Nobody could say for over twenty years.

scenes.label: 100% dog
scenes.say: Then this year, scientists pulled nuclear DNA from one of those pups. One geneticist said, it's one hundred percent a dog.

scenes.label: 15,800 years
scenes.say: And its age? About fifteen thousand eight hundred years. Before that, the oldest dog confirmed by DNA was only about ten thousand nine hundred years old.

scenes.label: +5,000 years
scenes.say: That pushes the record back roughly five thousand years. Into the Ice Age, when everyone was a hunter-gatherer.

scenes.label: First of all
scenes.say: Some experts say that means dogs may have been tamed more than ten thousand years before any other animal or plant.

scenes.label: Gough's Cave
scenes.say: Another ancient dog turned up in Gough's Cave in England, about fourteen thousand three hundred years old.

scenes.label: Tiny next to wolves
scenes.say: Scientists say its small size was the first clue. Wolves back then were exceptionally big.

scenes.label: Holes in the jaw
scenes.say: Some of those jawbones even had holes made on purpose by people. Researchers think these dogs mattered, even after death.

scenes.label: Fish diet
scenes.say: And look at this. Chemical tests showed the Turkish dogs ate a diet rich in fish, just like the people there.

scenes.label: Fed by people
scenes.say: Researchers think dogs weren't catching all that fish themselves. People were feeding them. Sound familiar?

scenes.label: Boxers and salukis
scenes.say: Plus, those Ice Age dogs were closer to the ancestors of breeds like boxers and salukis than to huskies.

scenes.label: Buried with people
scenes.say: So big dog family lines already existed fifteen thousand years ago. And at a nearby village, dogs were later buried right alongside people.

scenes.label: Bonus fact
scenes.say: Okay, quick bonus while we're here. We later bred dogs in every size. And that came with a price.

scenes.label: Big dogs age faster
scenes.say: Giant breeds like the Irish wolfhound often live ten years or less, on average. Tiny breeds tend to live much longer.

scenes.label: 894 dogs studied
scenes.say: A study of eight hundred ninety-four dogs found big dogs collect aging marks on their DNA faster. One researcher's grandma's chihuahua lived about twenty years.
So we know when dogs showed up. But here's the real mystery. How do you turn a wild, biting animal into a friend at all?

scenes.label: Siberia, 1959
scenes.say: Number one. In 1959, in Siberia, a scientist named Dmitry Belyaev tried to make a fox into a dog. On purpose.

scenes.label: Only the friendliest
scenes.say: His rule was simple. In each generation, only the calmest, friendliest foxes got to have pups. Nothing else counted.

scenes.label: Lyudmila Trut
scenes.say: His young assistant, Lyudmila Trut, was just twenty-five. She ended up running the experiment for decades.

scenes.label: 45,000 foxes
scenes.say: Over about forty years, the project went through roughly forty-five thousand foxes. That is a lot of very patient science.

scenes.label: 6 generations
scenes.say: After about six generations, some pups wagged their tails, whined for people, and licked hands like puppies.

scenes.label: 2% to ~50%
scenes.say: They called them the elite. Under two percent of pups by generation six. Eighteen percent by ten. About half by generation thirty.

scenes.label: Floppy ears
scenes.say: And then their bodies started changing too. Some got floppy ears, curly tails and patchy coats, like mutts.

scenes.label: Half the stress
scenes.say: By generation fifteen, their stress hormones were about half of normal farm foxes. Wild animals, slowly turning soft.

scenes.label: Still debated
scenes.say: Now, to be fair, a 2020 study pointed out some of those looks may have already existed in farm foxes before. Scientists still argue about it.

scenes.label: What changed inside?
scenes.say: But the friendliness itself? That was real. And for decades, nobody knew exactly what had changed inside their heads.

scenes.label: 9 fox brains
scenes.say: Until this week. On November second, Cornell scientists published a look inside nine fox brains. Tame, aggressive, and normal.

scenes.label: 'Attack' cells
scenes.say: They checked one spot near the base of the brain. In mice, switching on certain cells there makes a mouse attack, instantly.

scenes.label: Fewer 'attack' cells
scenes.say: And the tame foxes? They had fewer of those attack-linked brain cells than the other foxes.

scenes.label: First clue
scenes.say: So breeding for friendliness may have literally turned down part of the brain's aggression wiring. Only nine brains, so it's a first clue.

scenes.label: Turned down
scenes.say: And think about what that means for dogs. Maybe the wolf didn't vanish. Maybe it just got turned down.
So, back to my question. Did dogs choose us, or did we build them? Tell me in the comments. Which secret surprised you most?

short.title: Tame Foxes Have Fewer 'Attack' Brain Cells
short.header: How friendliness shows up in the brain
short.description: Foxes bred for friendliness since 1959 have fewer of the brain cells that, in mice, trigger attacks — a Cornell study published Nov 2, 2026 (Current Biology). Full story on how a wolf became your dog on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Your dog's friendliness might be wired in. Tame foxes have fewer attack-linked brain cells.

scenes.label: Siberia, 1959
scenes.say: Since 1959, scientists in Siberia let only the friendliest foxes have pups. After six generations, some pups wagged and licked hands like dogs.

scenes.label: Mice attack
scenes.say: In mice, switching on certain cells near the base of the brain makes a mouse attack instantly.

scenes.label: 9 brains
scenes.say: So Cornell scientists sliced up nine fox brains and counted. The tame foxes had fewer of those exact cells than the aggressive and wild ones.

scenes.label: Maybe our dogs too
scenes.say: It's a small study, but it might show how a wolf turned into your dog. Friendliness may live in that wiring.

scenes.label: Full story on my channel
scenes.say: So is your dog's friendliness wired in? Maybe. Because tame foxes have fewer attack-linked brain cells.
